notes: Original authored revision questions, not official exam questions or exam dumps.
Topics 1 and 2 were supplied in earlier chat responses and are not included in this download.
Topics 3-7 retain 25 questions per difficulty; Topics 8-30 have 15 per difficulty. This is not a 25-per-level bank for every topic.

Core concepts are deliberately revisited at different levels with distinct question stems. Beginner focuses on recognition; intermediate on application; advanced on scenario interpretation. Difficulty labels are editorial, not psychometrically calibrated.
Every question has four choices, one correct index and an explanation usable after either a correct or incorrect answer. The correct index is zero-based: 0=A, 1=B, 2=C, 3=D.

Scenarios are invented practice examples, not claims about actual workplace incidents. Commands depend on platform/software support. Production changes require the applicable approval and recovery process.
Sources are reference pointers for topic scope and technical review; the exam-topic outline is a scope reference, not detailed documentation for every answer.
This bank supplements practical labs and the official syllabus; it does not guarantee exam readiness or exhaust every possible question.

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Which medium carries data as light rather than electrical signals?
questions.explanation: Fibre uses optical signals. Copper carries electrical signals, so its interference characteristics differ from fibre.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Which fibre type is generally intended for longer-distance optical links when suitable optics are used?
answers: Any multimode fibre regardless of optics
questions.explanation: Single-mode fibre supports long-distance optical designs. Actual reach still depends on the transceiver and fibre specification, not the fibre label alone.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does multimode describe in optical fibre?
answers: Multiple IP subnets in one cable
Multiple propagation modes within the fibre
questions.explanation: Multimode concerns how light propagates through the fibre. It does not describe VLANs, addressing or Ethernet duplex.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What is a pluggable transceiver used for?
answers: Providing a compatible physical interface between a port and its medium
questions.explanation: A transceiver interfaces the port with the physical medium. Routing and addressing are separate functions.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does full duplex mean on an Ethernet link?
answers: Only one end can transmit at a time
Both ends can transmit and receive simultaneously
The link must use two VLANs
The link has two IP addresses
questions.explanation: Full duplex permits simultaneous transmission in both directions. It is not a statement about VLAN count or IP addressing.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does half duplex mean?
answers: Only half the VLANs are permitted
Transmission is shared so simultaneous sending can cause collisions
The cable is exactly half its normal length
Every packet loses half its payload
questions.explanation: Half-duplex Ethernet shares the transmission opportunity. Collisions are associated with this shared operation, not ordinary full-duplex Ethernet.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: On which Ethernet operating mode is CSMA/CD relevant?
answers: Every fibre link regardless of mode
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD manages access to a shared half-duplex medium. Collision detection is disabled in normal full-duplex Ethernet.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What is an Ethernet collision?
answers: Overlapping transmissions on a shared half-duplex medium
Two hosts having the same DNS suffix
questions.explanation: A collision concerns competing transmissions on shared Ethernet. Duplicate addressing is a different problem.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does an increasing CRC error counter indicate?
answers: Received frames failing their integrity check
questions.explanation: CRC errors indicate corrupted received frames. They justify investigating the physical path and related settings, but do not identify one component by themselves.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Which command normally provides detailed interface counters on Cisco IOS?
questions.explanation: show interfaces includes physical state and traffic/error counters. The other commands answer different operational questions.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does administratively down normally indicate?
answers: The interface is disabled in configuration
The interface is blocked by every ACL
questions.explanation: Administratively down normally means shutdown is configured. It is distinct from an enabled interface that cannot establish a physical link.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An enabled interface is down/down. What has not been established?
questions.explanation: Down/down indicates the interface is not operational. It does not alone distinguish a cable fault, remote shutdown or other physical dependency.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does a link showing up/up establish?
questions.explanation: Up/up is useful link evidence, not end-to-end service validation. VLAN, IP, routing and policy faults can still exist.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What is a speed mismatch?
answers: The router has two default routes
The two ends have incompatible operating speed settings
Two hosts use different DNS servers
questions.explanation: Both ends must operate compatibly. Speed settings concern the link, not application names or route count.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What is a duplex mismatch?
answers: One end uses a private IP
One end operates full duplex while the other operates half duplex
questions.explanation: Different duplex operation can produce errors and poor performance. Different hostnames or private addresses do not constitute duplex mismatch.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Why test a suspected patch lead with a known-good compatible lead?
answers: To prove every upstream route is correct
To isolate whether that segment contributes to the fault
To increase the configured VLAN range
questions.explanation: Controlled substitution tests a specific physical segment. It does not validate unrelated network services.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does a patch panel normally provide?
answers: A termination and cross-connection point for cabling
questions.explanation: A patch panel organises physical cable connections. It is not an active routing or application service.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Which medium is not affected by electromagnetic interference in the same way as copper?
questions.explanation: Fibre transports light rather than an electrical data signal. Optical links still have other faults such as attenuation or dirty connectors.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does link flapping mean?
answers: Repeated transitions between operational and non-operational link state
questions.explanation: Flapping describes repeated link-state changes. Logs and counters help determine when and where they occur.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Why inspect both ends of a link during troubleshooting?
answers: Either end or the connecting medium can affect operation
Only the local port can ever fail
questions.explanation: A link depends on both interfaces and the medium. One-sided evidence can miss a remote configuration or transmitter fault.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What is the purpose of an Ethernet frame check sequence?
questions.explanation: The FCS provides an integrity check for the frame. It is not encryption or user authentication.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Which observation most directly suggests a physical connection issue?
answers: An application returning an HTTP error
A user entering an incorrect password
questions.explanation: Loss of signal concerns the physical link. Application and authentication errors can occur on otherwise healthy links.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Why must optic and cable specifications be checked together?
answers: All optics use the same wavelength
The combination determines supported operation and reach
questions.explanation: Connector fit alone is insufficient. Speed, fibre type, wavelength, reach and platform support must be compatible.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: What does a port's negotiated speed describe?
answers: The operating data rate of that link
The guaranteed throughput of every application
The WAN provider's entire network capacity
questions.explanation: Link rate is one limit in the path. Application throughput also depends on overhead, congestion, endpoints and other links.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: How should an optical transmitter be inspected safely?
answers: View the laser through a magnifying glass
Use approved inspection procedures and equipment without looking into live fibre
questions.explanation: Optical transmitters can present an eye hazard. Follow approved laser-safe inspection and isolation procedures.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: CRC errors rise from 10 to 210 in five minutes while DNS resolves correctly. Which investigation is most relevant?
answers: The receiving physical path and interface settings
questions.explanation: The increasing CRC count is current frame-corruption evidence. Working DNS does not explain or remove those errors.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A port has 500 CRC errors, unchanged during a monitored test. What can you conclude?
answers: The DNS server caused all 500 errors
The port must be half duplex
The total includes historical errors; no new CRC errors were observed in that test
questions.explanation: A cumulative total is not an error rate. Compare counters over a defined interval before diagnosing an active fault.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A Fast Ethernet link shows half duplex at one end and full duplex at the other. What is wrong?
answers: Both ends must use different speeds
The route metric is too low
questions.explanation: The supplied settings directly establish duplex mismatch. Correcting it requires compatible configuration at both ends, with appropriate change control.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A gigabit-capable PC and switch negotiate 100 Mbps. Which check is relevant?
answers: Cable pair integrity and supported settings at both ends
The number of DNS A records
questions.explanation: Copper gigabit operation depends on a suitable complete cabling path and compatible endpoints. A lower negotiated speed is not proof of a DNS fault.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A PC works with the same cable on port 2 but not port 1. What is best isolated next?
questions.explanation: The test narrows the difference to the original port or its configuration. It does not yet prove a hardware failure.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A PC works through a replacement patch lead, with all other variables unchanged. What does this support?
answers: The original lead or its connection contributed to the fault
questions.explanation: Controlled substitution supports a fault in the changed segment. It does not establish a network-wide cause.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An enabled local port is down and the remote port is shutdown. Which correction addresses the known dependency?
answers: Clear the local ARP table only
Enable the remote port through approved change control
questions.explanation: The remote shutdown prevents normal link operation. Routing or ARP changes cannot enable the remote physical interface.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An interface is up/up with rising output drops but zero new CRC errors. Which explanation is more consistent?
questions.explanation: Output drops and CRC errors describe different failure mechanisms. Queue evidence points towards congestion rather than proving physical corruption.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A 1 Gbps port has low average utilisation but brief output drops. What should you consider?
answers: Short bursts can exceed available queue capacity
Low average utilisation proves no congestion
CRC must increase whenever output drops occur
questions.explanation: An average can hide microbursts. Examine queue and traffic evidence rather than treating the average as a complete picture.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A fibre link is down after moving patch cords. What should be verified before replacing switches?
answers: Correct patching, polarity, connector condition and compatible optics
questions.explanation: The change affected the physical path. Verify that path and its optical requirements before assuming switch failure.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An optic's specified receive range is -15 to -3 dBm; measured receive power is -18 dBm. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: More negative dBm means lower power. -18 dBm is below the supplied -15 dBm minimum; investigate loss and the remote transmitter.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An optic's receive range is -15 to -3 dBm; measured power is -1 dBm. What is the concern?
answers: Receive power exceeds the stated maximum
The IP subnet is too small
The reading is inside the range
questions.explanation: The supplied maximum is -3 dBm. -1 dBm is stronger and can exceed the receiver's supported input range.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Two optics fit the same socket but support different Ethernet rates. What must be checked?
answers: Port and optic support for a common operating rate
Whether their labels have the same colour
questions.explanation: Mechanical fit is not enough. The port, transceiver and peer must support compatible operation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A transceiver is not recognised after insertion. Which evidence is most useful?
questions.explanation: Recognition depends on supported hardware and software as well as correct insertion. Check the actual platform rather than guessing from connector shape.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An interface description says Printer but discovery shows an uplink switch. What should you verify?
answers: Assume discovery can never be correct
Disable it immediately because the description is authoritative
Actual patching and neighbour information before changing the port
questions.explanation: Descriptions can be stale. Correlate physical mapping and live evidence to avoid changing an unexpected uplink.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A full-duplex link is currently stable but shows old collision counters. What is the sound next step?
answers: Assume all full-duplex traffic uses CSMA/CD
Declare active collisions solely from the total
Check whether counters increase and verify their history/meaning
questions.explanation: Normal full duplex does not use collision detection. Historical or platform-specific counters require careful interpretation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A wall port maps to a different switch interface than the documentation states. Which problem is established?
answers: The WAN has no default route
The documented physical mapping is inaccurate
questions.explanation: The mapping evidence concerns patching/documentation. It does not prove a DHCP or WAN failure.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A fibre link uses a transmit strand and a receive strand. What pairing is required?
answers: Both receive ports must be joined
Each transmitter must reach the opposite receiver
questions.explanation: A duplex optical link needs transmit-to-receive continuity. Incorrect polarity can prevent signal reception.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A link works until a cabinet door presses sharply on the fibre. Which investigation fits?
answers: Bend radius and physical stress on the fibre
questions.explanation: The symptom correlates with physical stress. Follow the cable's handling specification rather than changing unrelated protocols.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A port's input CRC counter increases. Which direction is directly implicated by that counter?
answers: Only frames transmitted from that port
questions.explanation: Input CRC records receive-side integrity failures. The cause can lie in the remote transmitter, medium or local receiver.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A link reports up/up but the PC is in the wrong VLAN. Which statement is correct?
answers: Link operation and service configuration are separate
VLAN faults must make the physical link down
Up/up proves the VLAN is correct
questions.explanation: Physical state does not validate VLAN placement. Both can be checked independently.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A cable tester reports an open conductor. What has been found?
questions.explanation: The test identifies a conductor problem. Higher-layer configuration changes do not repair physical continuity.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A port is shutdown in the running configuration. Which command normally enables it under interface configuration?
questions.explanation: no shutdown removes administrative disablement. Use it only after verifying the intended port and required approval.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A link flaps exactly when a device is rebooted. What is the most cautious conclusion?
answers: The WAN provider is certainly responsible
The events correlate with the remote reboot and should be checked against its logs
The local switch must be replaced
questions.explanation: A remote reboot can remove link signal. Correlation narrows the investigation but does not justify an unsupported hardware diagnosis.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Both link ends support autonegotiation and no exception is required. Which approach avoids a mixed forced/automatic setup?
answers: Force one end full and leave the other half
Use compatible autonegotiation at both ends
questions.explanation: Compatible negotiation avoids one-sided settings. Forced operation, where needed, must be coordinated and supported at both ends.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: At 10:00 a port has 1,000 CRC errors; at 10:10 it has 1,000 after 2 million additional frames. What is supported?
answers: The port has never had a fault
No new CRC errors were observed in that interval
questions.explanation: Counter differences, not the absolute total, establish observed activity. This interval does not erase historical faults or validate applications.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: During a test, input frames increase by 100,000 and CRC errors by 200. What is the observed CRC error proportion?
questions.explanation: 200 divided by 100,000 is 0.002, or 0.2 percent. Use the same interval for numerator and denominator.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: End A is 100/full; end B is 100/half and records late collisions. Which explanation best fits?
questions.explanation: The explicit duplex disagreement explains the half-duplex side's collision symptoms. Late collisions warrant investigation rather than being treated as normal contention.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A 100 Mbps half-duplex interface records ordinary collisions under load but no late collisions. What is the correct interpretation?
answers: All collisions are normal on full duplex
Ordinary collisions can occur on shared half-duplex Ethernet
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD handles contention on half-duplex Ethernet. Distinguish normal collision behaviour from late/excessive collision faults.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A verified full-duplex link reports rapidly increasing collision counters inconsistent with hardware operation. What is the best next investigation?
answers: Validate platform counter semantics, software issues and actual link settings
questions.explanation: Normal full duplex disables collision detection. Inconsistent evidence should trigger validation, not an invented half-duplex explanation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A receives -20 dBm; its stated minimum is -16 dBm. B's transmitter is within its specified range. What remains plausible?
answers: A proven B transmitter failure despite normal evidence
Excessive path loss or a receive-side issue
questions.explanation: Normal remote transmit power does not prove acceptable received power. Inspect the path and receiver with safe procedures.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A's transmitter is -2 dBm and B receives -8 dBm. Ignoring measurement uncertainty, what is the path loss?
questions.explanation: The power difference is -2 minus -8, giving 6 dB loss. Compare it with the supplied design budget before judging acceptability.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A design allows 8 dB loss. Fibre loss is 4 dB, connectors 2 dB and splices 1 dB. What margin remains?
questions.explanation: Total specified loss is 7 dB, leaving 1 dB against the 8 dB budget. This is a calculation from the scenario, not a universal optical limit.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Two compatible optics have receiver range -18 to -4 dBm. The link receives -2 dBm. Which proposed action requires evaluation?
answers: Add amplification because the signal is weak
Use a correctly specified attenuation solution if the design calls for it
Increase the Ethernet MTU to reduce optical power
questions.explanation: The reading is stronger than the allowed maximum. Any attenuation must be designed for the actual optics and path, not applied blindly.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A fibre link works in A-to-B direction but B-to-A signal is absent. Which scope best fits?
answers: B transmitter, return strand, patching or A receiver
questions.explanation: Optical directions have separate components. One working direction does not validate the opposite transmitter/strand/receiver path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Replacing only the local optic does not change low receive power. What is justified?
answers: The local replacement did not resolve the symptom; inspect remaining path and peer evidence
The remote optic is definitely faulty
questions.explanation: A negative substitution result narrows evidence but does not uniquely identify the remote component. Continue controlled isolation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: An optic's maximum specified reach is 300 m on the installed fibre grade; the measured run is 450 m. What is established?
answers: The installation exceeds the supplied reach specification
The link is guaranteed reliable if it comes up
The IP address must be invalid
questions.explanation: A link light does not override the design specification. Evaluate a supported optic/fibre solution for the actual distance.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A port supports 10 Gbps only; a 1 Gbps optic fits but is unsupported. What explains failure to establish the intended link?
answers: No supported common port/optic operating mode
questions.explanation: Form-factor fit does not establish rate compatibility. Use the actual port and transceiver support matrix.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Both optical ends have correct power but incompatible FEC settings for the stated high-speed link. What should be checked?
questions.explanation: Optical power is one requirement. High-speed links can also depend on encoding/FEC compatibility; this is an industry-extension diagnostic.
questions.scope: Industry extension

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A's input CRC rises; B's input CRC remains zero. What is the strongest conclusion?
answers: Corruption is observed in the B-to-A receive direction, without uniquely identifying the failed component
questions.explanation: The receiving counter identifies where bad frames are observed. The source can be the peer transmitter, medium or local receiver.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: CRC remains zero while output drops rise during bursts. Which change is most directly relevant to investigate?
answers: Traffic demand, egress capacity and queue behaviour
Replacing fibre solely because of CRC evidence
questions.explanation: The evidence points towards egress queue pressure. A physical replacement needs physical evidence, not merely any packet-loss symptom.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A 1 Gbps egress receives 1.5 Gbps offered traffic for a sustained interval. Without enough buffering or flow control, what is expected?
answers: Guaranteed zero loss because the link is full duplex
A DNS timeout is the only possible symptom
questions.explanation: Offered traffic exceeds service capacity. Full duplex separates directions but does not remove the egress bandwidth limit.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: Two redundant uplinks share one damaged patch panel. Why can both fail?
answers: They retain a common physical dependency
questions.explanation: Logical or port redundancy does not imply physically independent infrastructure. Check the full physical route.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A long-lived counter was reset during testing. Which comparison is invalid without accounting for that reset?
answers: Subtracting the old total from the post-reset total as one continuous interval
questions.explanation: Counter discontinuity breaks naive subtraction. Preserve timestamps and reset information so rates are meaningful.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A port flaps and logs transceiver removal at the same moments. Which hypothesis is best supported?
answers: Intermittent module seating/detection or related hardware evidence
questions.explanation: The event concerns transceiver presence. Correlate seating, hardware and logs before making a definitive component diagnosis.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A replacement optic has matching rate and connector but a different unsupported wavelength pairing. Why can the link fail?
answers: The remote DNS server selects the laser
Optical compatibility includes wavelength, not just mechanical fit
questions.explanation: Optics must be compatible as a pair and with the medium. Matching connector and speed is not a complete check.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A single-fibre bidirectional link uses paired complementary optics. Two identical transmit/receive wavelength variants are installed. What is suspect?
answers: The VLAN mask is too short
The default route controls receive wavelength
Both must work because their labels match
The optics may not be the required complementary pair
questions.explanation: BiDi designs require the correct paired wavelength arrangement. Verify the specified pairing rather than assuming identical units are appropriate.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A replacement cable restores link speed but the application remains slow with clean physical counters. What should happen next?
answers: Continue higher-layer/path testing rather than declare all faults fixed
Assume the cable test proves application health
questions.explanation: One repaired symptom does not validate the whole service. Check routing, congestion, transport and application evidence next.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A cable path passes continuity testing but fails its required performance certification. What is correct?
answers: The performance test can be ignored if a link light exists
Any continuity pass guarantees all Ethernet speeds
Continuity alone does not establish performance at the required Ethernet rate
questions.explanation: A conductor can be connected yet fail signal-quality requirements. Validate the cabling against the required standard and installation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Cabling, optics, Ethernet connections and interface faults
questions.question: A live fibre fault must be investigated. Which method avoids unsafe inspection and preserves evidence?
answers: Look into the fibre while transmitting
Use approved isolation, inspection tools, optical readings and controlled changes
Clean a live connector while viewing the laser
questions.explanation: Laser-safe procedures and controlled changes are essential. Gather readings and follow approved isolation before handling optical connections.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Which transport protocol provides a reliable ordered byte stream?
questions.explanation: TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP does not itself guarantee ordered delivery.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Which transport protocol sends datagrams without establishing a TCP-style connection?
questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless at the transport layer. An application can still maintain its own session or reliability mechanisms.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What is the usual TCP connection-establishment sequence?
questions.explanation: The three-way handshake establishes TCP state and synchronises sequence information. It does not authenticate the application user.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does a transport port number identify in ordinary TCP/IP communication?
questions.explanation: Transport ports distinguish application endpoints on a host. They are not the same as physical network ports.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Which is a transport-layer protocol?
questions.explanation: TCP operates above IP and below applications. ARP and Ethernet serve local link functions; IPv4 provides network-layer delivery.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What is encapsulation?
answers: Assigning all hosts the same MAC
Converting every packet into a DNS record
Adding protocol information as data passes down the network stack
questions.explanation: Encapsulation wraps higher-layer data with lower-layer headers and, where relevant, trailers. Each layer provides its own function.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Which order describes a typical outbound TCP-over-IPv4 Ethernet packet?
questions.explanation: TCP carries application bytes, IP carries the TCP segment, and Ethernet carries the IP packet on the link.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What is an Ethernet frame?
answers: A link-layer unit carrying data and Ethernet addressing
questions.explanation: A frame is the local link-layer unit. It is distinct from an IP packet or a TCP segment.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What is an IP packet?
answers: A network-layer unit with IP addressing
questions.explanation: IP addressing supports delivery across networks. The packet can be carried by different link-layer technologies.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What is a TCP segment?
answers: A TCP header and associated payload
questions.explanation: TCP segments carry transport information and bytes. Ethernet frames and IP packets encapsulate them on the path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does a TCP acknowledgement normally indicate?
answers: The next sequence number the receiver expects
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledgement numbers track received byte-stream progress. They do not directly indicate application success.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does TCP retransmission do?
answers: Resends data believed lost or unacknowledged
questions.explanation: Retransmission supports reliable delivery when acknowledgements are absent or loss is detected. It adds delay and cannot guarantee a working path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Which statement about UDP is correct?
answers: UDP guarantees every datagram arrives once
UDP itself does not guarantee delivery or ordering
questions.explanation: UDP provides minimal transport mechanisms. Applications can add their own reliability or security above it.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Why might a real-time application use UDP?
answers: UDP removes the need for IP
It can avoid TCP's transport-level ordered-delivery delays
questions.explanation: Some real-time applications prefer timely delivery over waiting for missing data. This is an application trade-off, not a guarantee of speed.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does TCP flow control protect against?
questions.explanation: The receive window communicates capacity. Congestion control addresses network load, which is a separate concern.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does TCP congestion control respond to?
questions.explanation: Congestion control adjusts sending behaviour based on network feedback and inferred conditions. It is distinct from receiver flow control.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does a TCP FIN normally request?
answers: An orderly end to one direction of the byte stream
questions.explanation: FIN participates in orderly closure. A TCP reset is a different, abrupt termination mechanism.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does a TCP RST indicate?
questions.explanation: RST concerns TCP state. Its exact cause needs context; it does not uniquely prove a firewall or server fault.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Does successful ping prove TCP port 443 is reachable?
answers: Yes, every IP protocol shares one policy
No, ping tests a different protocol
Yes, if the destination is private
No, because ping never uses IP
questions.explanation: ICMP reachability and TCP service access are separate tests. Policy and application state can differ.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does a checksum provide?
questions.explanation: Checksums support integrity detection, not encryption or identity verification. Different protocols have different checksum rules.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What is decapsulation?
answers: Removing and interpreting protocol wrapping at the receiving layers
questions.explanation: The receiving stack processes each layer's information and passes the payload upward. This reverses encapsulation conceptually.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does a TCP source port commonly distinguish?
questions.explanation: Client source ports often distinguish simultaneous connections. They are transport identifiers, not physical port labels.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Which statement about encryption is correct?
answers: Neither ordinary TCP nor ordinary UDP inherently encrypts application data
TCP always encrypts and UDP never can
questions.explanation: Encryption comes from additional protocols or applications. Transport choice alone does not establish confidentiality.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Can an application built on UDP implement acknowledgements?
answers: Only if Ethernet is half duplex
questions.explanation: UDP lacks built-in reliable delivery, but applications can implement acknowledgements and retransmission themselves.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: What does TCP preserve for the application?
answers: Every router hop as a message
An ordered byte stream, not application message boundaries
Every send call as a separate message
questions.explanation: TCP delivers bytes in order without preserving application write boundaries. Applications must define their own framing.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A client sends SYN and receives SYN-ACK. What normally completes the handshake?
questions.explanation: The client's ACK completes ordinary TCP establishment. This does not yet establish that the application transaction succeeds.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A capture shows repeated SYNs with no replies. What is justified?
answers: The application has authenticated the user
The client has not observed a response establishing the connection
The server definitely has no power
questions.explanation: The observation does not uniquely locate the loss or filtering point. Compare path and endpoint evidence.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A SYN reaches a host and the host replies with RST. What is a plausible interpretation?
answers: The client has received all application data
The link must be half duplex
The connection was rejected, for example because no service listens there
questions.explanation: RST is an explicit reset/rejection. Confirm the listener and policy; do not equate it with silent packet loss.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A TCP connection is established but the application returns an error. What is established?
answers: Transport connectivity worked for that exchange, not application success
questions.explanation: A successful transport session can carry an application error. Diagnose the layer indicated by the actual response.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A server receives bytes 1000 through 1499 in order. What acknowledgement number is expected next, ignoring wraparound?
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledges the next expected byte. Five hundred bytes starting at 1000 end at 1499.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A segment starts at sequence 2000 and carries 300 data bytes. What is the next data sequence number?
questions.explanation: TCP sequence numbers count bytes. The next data byte follows the 300-byte range ending at 2299.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A SYN uses sequence 500. What acknowledgement covers that SYN?
questions.explanation: SYN consumes one sequence number even without application payload. This is separate from ordinary data-byte counting.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A FIN uses sequence 900 after all preceding bytes. What acknowledgement covers that FIN?
questions.explanation: FIN consumes one sequence number. It marks orderly end-of-stream for that direction.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Two clients connect to the same server TCP port 443. How can their sessions be distinguished?
questions.explanation: A TCP connection is identified by its endpoint address/port pair. One listening port can serve many distinct sessions.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A receiver advertises a zero TCP window. What does this indicate?
answers: The server has no IP address
It currently advertises no capacity for additional ordinary data
questions.explanation: Zero window concerns receiver flow control. The network may still be reachable and the connection still exist.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A capture shows a retransmission. Does that prove the physical cable is faulty?
answers: No, loss or missing acknowledgement can have several causes
Yes, every retransmission is a CRC fault
No, retransmission proves there was no loss
Yes, if TCP port 443 is used
questions.explanation: Transport symptoms require correlation with interface, path and endpoint evidence. Retransmission alone does not identify a cable.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: An application needs reliable ordered delivery and does not implement its own recovery. Which transport is the stronger fit?
answers: UDP solely because it is shorter
questions.explanation: TCP supplies the required transport behaviour. UDP would require additional application mechanisms for those guarantees.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A live audio application tolerates some loss but cannot wait for late data. Which transport characteristic may favour UDP?
answers: No built-in ordered-stream recovery blocking later datagrams
questions.explanation: UDP leaves timing/recovery choices to the application. It does not itself guarantee quality or capacity.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A UDP datagram reaches a host but the application is not listening. What response may be observed in IPv4?
questions.explanation: ICMP may report the unavailable UDP port. Filtering or implementation behaviour can suppress the response, so silence is not proof of openness.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A host sends to a remote subnet without NAT. Which destination stays the remote host across ordinary routing?
answers: The destination MAC on every link
questions.explanation: IP destination identifies the end host. Ethernet addresses and checksums are rebuilt for each link.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A packet crosses an Ethernet router without NAT. What normally changes in the next Ethernet frame?
answers: The destination application port solely due to routing
The original application payload solely due to routing
questions.explanation: The router builds a new frame for the next link. Ordinary routing does not inherently change transport ports or application data.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A PC sends to an off-subnet server. Which local address does it normally resolve with ARP?
answers: The remote server's MAC across the WAN
Its selected next-hop gateway's IPv4 address
questions.explanation: ARP resolves local-link next-hop addressing. It does not discover remote MAC addresses across ordinary routed boundaries.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A UDP datagram has 100 payload bytes. What is its length including the standard UDP header?
questions.explanation: The standard UDP header is eight bytes. UDP length includes header and payload, not the surrounding IP/Ethernet headers.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A TCP segment has no options. What is the minimum TCP header length?
questions.explanation: The base TCP header is 20 bytes. Options can increase it; UDP's standard header is eight bytes.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: An application writes two short messages into TCP. Can the receiver assume two reads will return exactly those messages?
answers: Yes, Ethernet frames preserve every application write
Only if both hosts share DNS
Yes, TCP preserves each write as one message
questions.explanation: TCP is a byte stream. Segmentation and reads need not align with application writes.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A packet has TTL 1 when a router processes it for forwarding. What normally happens?
answers: The router expires it rather than forwarding it onward
It gains a TTL of 255 automatically
The router asks DNS to extend it
questions.explanation: Routers decrement TTL. Expiration prevents indefinite circulation and can produce ICMP Time Exceeded.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A TCP port test succeeds but a login fails. Which next focus is most justified?
answers: Replace fibre solely from the login error
questions.explanation: The port test establishes a narrower network fact. Login success depends on additional application and identity functions.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: An ACL permits ICMP but denies TCP 443. Which observation is consistent?
answers: Ping succeeds while HTTPS connections fail
questions.explanation: Different protocols can receive different policy treatment. Successful ping does not prove permission for HTTPS.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A TCP receiver acknowledges data. Does that necessarily mean the application committed it to a database?
answers: Yes, TCP ACK guarantees database durability
No, because TCP never acknowledges bytes
Yes, if the connection is encrypted
No, transport acknowledgement is not application commit confirmation
questions.explanation: Transport delivery and application processing are different layers. Use an application response to establish transaction outcome.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: An application sends a UDP request and times out. Which statement is justified?
answers: No expected application reply was observed; the cause is not yet identified
The UDP port is definitely closed
questions.explanation: UDP silence is ambiguous. Check captures, listener state and policy rather than inventing a unique cause.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Client SYN is visible at the client but absent in a simultaneous server capture. What scope is supported?
answers: The server application's response processing only
The outbound path or capture visibility between those points
questions.explanation: The captures localise where evidence disappears, subject to capture placement and accuracy. They do not uniquely identify one intermediate device.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Server SYN-ACK is visible at the server but absent at the client. What should be investigated?
answers: A missing SYN at the server despite the capture
The return path and filtering between the capture points
questions.explanation: The server responded, but the client did not observe it. Return routing, policy or loss are relevant next checks.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Both endpoints capture the handshake, then the server sends an application error. What is best supported?
answers: The observed transport exchange worked; investigate the application error
The client has no working route
questions.explanation: The response is evidence of application-layer failure over an established transport. It does not prove every later flow or dependency works.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Bytes 1000-1499 and 2000-2499 arrive; bytes 1500-1999 are missing. Without SACK detail, what cumulative ACK is expected?
questions.explanation: Cumulative acknowledgement advances only through contiguous bytes. Out-of-order later data does not fill the gap.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A TCP receiver acknowledges 5000, then repeatedly acknowledges 5000 after later data arrives. What does this commonly suggest?
answers: Successful acknowledgement of every later byte cumulatively
A gap before the next expected byte
questions.explanation: Repeated cumulative ACKs can signal missing data. Interpret them with sequence ranges and capture context rather than assuming one cause.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A capture records a checksum error on an outbound packet before NIC offload completes. What must be considered?
answers: Capture/offload artefacts before declaring wire corruption
The DNS server generated the TCP checksum
All such packets must be corrupt on the wire
questions.explanation: Host captures can see checksums before hardware completion. Validate offload context or an external capture before diagnosing corruption.
questions.scope: Industry extension

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A TCP stream has an established session and a zero receive window, with clean interface counters. Which bottleneck is directly advertised?
questions.explanation: The receiver explicitly advertises no ordinary receive capacity. Investigate endpoint/application consumption while keeping other evidence in view.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: The receiver window is large, but loss causes TCP to reduce its sending rate. Which mechanism is involved?
questions.explanation: Congestion control adjusts sending based on network conditions. A large receive window does not guarantee a congestion-free path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A single TCP segment is lost while later segments arrive. Why can delivery of later bytes to the application wait?
answers: TCP converts later segments to DNS
The receiver cannot store any out-of-order data
questions.explanation: Ordered delivery waits for missing earlier bytes, even if later bytes are buffered. This is a transport trade-off relevant to real-time applications.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A UDP-based application numbers messages and requests missing ones again. Which statement is correct?
answers: UDP has become TCP at the IP layer
Ethernet automatically supplies the message numbers
questions.explanation: Applications can build reliability over UDP. Distinguish application behaviour from UDP's own minimal guarantees.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Two sessions share source/destination IPs and destination TCP port, but have different source ports. Are they distinguishable?
answers: Only if they use different cables
No, destination port alone identifies a session
Only if their VLAN names differ
Yes, their TCP endpoint tuples differ
questions.explanation: The source port is part of the connection identity. Multiple sessions can reach one listening service.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A NAT device changes a packet's source IP and TCP source port. What additional integrity information needs appropriate updating?
questions.explanation: Checksums cover changed header information, including TCP's IP pseudo-header. Translation must preserve packet validity.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A routed IPv4 packet's TTL changes but its TCP data and addresses do not. Which checksum changes because of TTL alone?
answers: TCP checksum solely because TTL changed
questions.explanation: TTL is in the IPv4 header, not the TCP pseudo-header. Ordinary TTL decrement changes the IPv4 header checksum.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A host capture sees a large TCP offload buffer larger than link MTU. What should be considered before claiming oversized wire frames?
answers: Every router must accept that exact frame
Segmentation offload may divide it before transmission
questions.explanation: Host-side offload can change what captures show. Compare wire-level evidence and interface capabilities before diagnosing MTU violations.
questions.scope: Industry extension

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: Small TCP exchanges work but large transfers stall; a smaller-MSS test works. What hypothesis is strengthened?
answers: A path MTU or segmentation-related issue
questions.explanation: Size-sensitive behaviour and the controlled MSS test support an MTU-related investigation. They do not alone identify the exact blocking device.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A path drops required ICMP fragmentation-needed messages and cannot carry the larger DF-set packets. What can result?
answers: A path MTU discovery black hole
questions.explanation: The sender may not learn the smaller path limit. Small packets can work while larger DF-set packets fail.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: TCP SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK complete, then a firewall resets the flow with a recorded policy action. What identifies the observed cause?
answers: The matching reset action and flow evidence
Handshake success proves policy can never act later
Only the source port's numeric size
questions.explanation: An established session can still be terminated by policy. Correlate the specific action with the captured flow.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A client receives a TCP RST whose IP source resembles the server. Does that alone prove the server application generated it?
answers: No, an intermediate device may generate or inject a reset
Yes, source IP alone is conclusive
Yes, every reset is a successful login
No, TCP resets never have IP addresses
questions.explanation: Reset attribution requires endpoint and path evidence. Address appearance alone does not establish the generating component.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A SYN is retransmitted three times, then succeeds. What is the strongest conclusion?
answers: Initial establishment attempts lacked the expected response; later establishment succeeded
The application was authenticated on the first attempt
The physical cable is conclusively faulty
questions.explanation: The sequence describes observed transport behaviour. Loss, filtering, endpoint delay or other causes need further evidence.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A receiver sends ACK 3001 after a FIN at sequence 3000. What does this establish?
answers: The peer has also finished sending all its own data
The FIN's sequence-space position was acknowledged
questions.explanation: TCP directions close independently. Acknowledging one FIN does not by itself establish closure of the opposite direction.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A connection's two directions carry different amounts of data. Must their sequence numbers advance equally?
answers: Yes, every connection uses one shared counter
Only if the server uses a private IP
No, each direction has independent sequence space
Yes, ACKs make both counters identical
questions.explanation: TCP tracks each direction separately. Bidirectional applications need not send equal byte counts.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A UDP datagram's checksum is present. Does that guarantee confidentiality or delivery?
answers: No, integrity detection is not encryption or reliable delivery
Yes, if the payload is short
questions.explanation: A checksum detects certain corruption. It does not conceal payload or guarantee arrival, order or uniqueness.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: An IPv4 UDP packet carries checksum zero. What does that field normally signify in basic UDP?
questions.explanation: Basic IPv4 UDP permits omission signalled by zero. Do not generalise this rule to ordinary IPv6 UDP, which has different requirements.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: A UDP length field is 28. With the standard header, how much UDP payload is present?
questions.explanation: UDP length includes its eight-byte header. Subtract eight to obtain the payload; surrounding IP headers are not included.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: TCP, UDP and encapsulation
questions.question: An application sends a request, receives TCP ACKs, but no application response before timeout. What remains unverified?
answers: Whether the source used an IP address
Whether any bytes reached the TCP receiver
Whether TCP exists on the server
Application processing and response, despite transport acknowledgements
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledgements are not application completion messages. Inspect server processing, dependencies and response-path evidence.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
questions.explanation: IPv4 has four eight-bit octets, totalling 32 bits. MAC and IPv6 address lengths are different.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which is valid dotted-decimal IPv4 notation?
questions.explanation: An IPv4 address has four octets, each from 0 to 255. The other choices have an invalid value or octet count.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does a subnet mask identify?
answers: Which address bits describe the network and host portions
questions.explanation: The mask divides the address into network and host portions. It does not itself supply a route or authenticate a user.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does /24 mean?
questions.explanation: Prefix length counts network bits. It is not the number of usable hosts or a required gateway address.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What is the purpose of a default gateway on a host?
answers: Providing a next hop for destinations without a more specific local route
questions.explanation: A gateway provides a path towards remote networks. Name resolution and address classification are separate functions.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which address is in RFC 1918 private space?
questions.explanation: 10.0.0.0/8 is private. Documentation and link-local ranges are special-use but are not RFC 1918 private ranges.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which is another RFC 1918 private address?
questions.explanation: The private 172 range is 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255. Not every address starting with 172 is private.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which 192-prefixed range is RFC 1918 private?
questions.explanation: Only the specified 192.168/16 range is RFC 1918 private here. Similar-looking prefixes have different uses.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What is 127.0.0.1 normally used for?
questions.explanation: Loopback refers to the local host. Reaching it does not test the physical LAN path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does a Windows DHCP client assigning itself 169.254.10.20 commonly indicate?
answers: It received a normal private DHCP lease
It did not obtain DHCP configuration
The internet gateway is confirmed healthy
questions.explanation: APIPA can provide local-link addressing after DHCP is unavailable. It does not uniquely prove the DHCP server itself failed.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What is a static IP configuration?
answers: An address that can never change physically
An address with no subnet mask
Addressing configured explicitly rather than leased dynamically
questions.explanation: Static configuration still needs correct mask, gateway and other settings. Static does not mean automatically valid.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does DHCP normally provide?
answers: Automatic addressing and related network options
questions.explanation: DHCP can provide an address, mask, gateway and DNS settings. Those supplied options must still be correct.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which Windows command displays detailed adapter IP settings?
questions.explanation: ipconfig /all exposes addressing, DNS and DHCP details. The other commands belong to network-device tasks.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which modern Linux command displays interface addresses?
questions.explanation: The ip utility displays Linux addressing. Do not assume Windows or Cisco IOS command syntax works on Linux.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which modern Linux command displays routes?
questions.explanation: ip route show displays routing information. DNS tools do not display the host's routing table.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does a DNS-server setting identify?
answers: The mandatory next hop for every packet
Where the client sends name-resolution queries
questions.explanation: DNS is a service destination. A DNS server is not automatically the default gateway.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Can two hosts communicate locally without a default gateway if they share a subnet and working VLAN?
answers: Only if both addresses are public
No, every frame must traverse a router
questions.explanation: Local communication normally does not need a gateway. Remote networks add a routing requirement.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What can duplicate IPv4 addresses on one LAN cause?
answers: Conflicting address ownership and intermittent connectivity
questions.explanation: Two devices claiming one address can disrupt ARP and delivery. This is not a supported redundancy arrangement by itself.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does a conventional subnet's network address identify?
answers: The first ordinary host by definition
questions.explanation: The network address has host bits zero. It is normally not assigned to an ordinary host in conventional subnets.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does a conventional subnet's directed broadcast address represent?
answers: All hosts in that subnet at the IP addressing level
questions.explanation: Broadcast has host bits one. Forwarding of directed broadcasts across routers is separately controlled and not assumed.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Does a private address mean the device is automatically secure?
answers: No, addressing scope is not a security policy
Yes, private addresses cannot be attacked
Yes, private hosts need no authentication
questions.explanation: Private addressing does not replace firewall policy, patching or access control. Security depends on additional controls.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Does a public-looking IPv4 address prove internet reachability?
answers: Yes, DNS is unnecessary for every application
Yes, the number guarantees a working ISP
No, routes and policy still matter
questions.explanation: An address alone does not establish connectivity. Correct allocation, forwarding, return paths and policy remain necessary.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What does a host normally use to decide whether a destination is on its local subnet?
answers: Its address and subnet mask, subject to its routing table
questions.explanation: Address and mask identify the connected network. More specific routes can alter the next-hop decision.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Must a default gateway always end in .1?
answers: No, it can be another valid reachable gateway address
Yes, DHCP cannot supply another value
Only private gateways must end in .1
questions.explanation: .1 is a convention, not a protocol requirement. The configured gateway must be valid and reachable for the design.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: What is the IPv4 limited broadcast address?
questions.explanation: 255.255.255.255 is limited broadcast on the local link. It is distinct from a particular subnet's directed broadcast.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 192.168.10.20/24. Which proposed gateway is on its connected subnet?
questions.explanation: The /24 connected network is 192.168.10.0/24. .254 is a valid host address there; this does not alone prove a router owns it.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 192.168.10.20/24 with no other routes. Is 192.168.10.200 local?
questions.explanation: Both addresses share the first 24 bits. DNS does not determine subnet membership.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 192.168.10.20/24. Is 192.168.11.20 on its connected subnet?
questions.explanation: The third octet differs under /24. A next hop is needed for the remote subnet unless another applicable route exists.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 10.1.4.20/23. Which address is in its connected subnet?
questions.explanation: 10.1.4.0/23 covers third octets 4 and 5. The supplied mask, not classful assumptions, determines membership.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A /24 client has gateway 192.168.20.1 but address 192.168.10.20, with no special on-link route. What is wrong?
answers: DNS must assign a new MAC
The gateway is outside its connected subnet
questions.explanation: The ordinary gateway must be reachable on the local link. The question excludes special routes that could change that assumption.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A PC reaches local peers but has no default or other remote routes. What is expected for an unrelated remote subnet?
answers: A physical link failure for every local peer
No usable host route to that destination
