questions.explanation: Local success does not supply remote routing. Check the host route table and intended gateway.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which address is outside RFC 1918 private space?
questions.explanation: The private 172 block ends at 172.31.255.255. 172.32 is outside it, though that alone does not prove a usable public allocation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which address is inside the private 172.16.0.0/12 range?
questions.explanation: The second octet spans 16 through 31. Similar first octets do not establish membership.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A Windows client has APIPA and no default gateway after DHCP fails. Which service can still be possible?
answers: Ordinary routed internet access through APIPA
Communication with suitable link-local peers on the same link
questions.explanation: Link-local addressing supports a limited local scope. It is not a replacement for routed addressing and gateway configuration.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A PC keeps its old static address after moving to another VLAN/subnet. What should be checked?
answers: Address, mask and gateway against the new subnet
questions.explanation: The physical link can work while addressing belongs to the old network. Validate all relevant IP parameters.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Two hosts have different MAC addresses but both claim 192.168.1.50. What evidence fits a duplicate-IP fault?
answers: ARP ownership alternates between the MACs
The DNS suffix is always blank
questions.explanation: Competing ARP claims can redirect traffic unpredictably. Distinct MACs do not make a duplicated IPv4 address safe.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A PC can ping its own loopback but not its gateway. What has loopback established?
answers: Some local stack operation, not LAN reachability
questions.explanation: Loopback does not traverse the physical network. Continue with adapter, addressing and local-path evidence.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A PC reaches a server by IP but its hostname fails to resolve. Which setting is most relevant?
answers: Configured DNS servers and name-resolution behaviour
questions.explanation: Direct-IP success and name failure point towards DNS. Verify queries and configured servers rather than changing unrelated settings.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A Windows adapter shows DHCP Enabled: No. What does that establish?
answers: The adapter has no MAC address
It is not currently configured to obtain its address by DHCP
The DHCP server is definitely offline
The client must be using IPv6 only
questions.explanation: The field describes client configuration. It does not diagnose the availability of the DHCP server.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A DHCP lease supplies the wrong gateway but correct address and mask. Which symptom fits?
answers: The client automatically repairs the gateway
The Ethernet link must be down
Every local ARP request must fail
Local subnet access works while remote access fails
questions.explanation: Local forwarding can work without the correct gateway. Remote destinations require the appropriate next hop.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Which Linux output most directly shows the selected default gateway?
questions.explanation: The default route identifies the next hop and interface. Address, MAC and DNS lines describe other parameters.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host has a correct mask but a wrong DNS server. Does that alone change which IP destinations it considers on-link?
answers: Yes, DNS determines the Ethernet duplex
Yes, DNS replaces the subnet mask
Only when the host uses TCP
No, DNS and connected-subnet classification are separate
questions.explanation: DNS can affect which address a name resolves to, but does not itself rewrite the host's connected prefix.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 192.168.1.130/25. Which ordinary gateway is valid on that subnet?
questions.explanation: The subnet is .128-.255, with .128 network and .255 broadcast. .129 is usable; .1 is outside and .128 is not an ordinary host.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 192.168.1.70/26. Which address is its subnet's broadcast?
questions.explanation: The /26 block is .64-.127. The last address is broadcast; .64 is network and .128 starts the next block.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Two hosts share a VLAN but belong to different IP subnets. Is sharing the VLAN alone sufficient for ordinary direct IP communication?
answers: Only if both names are short
No, appropriate Layer 3 addressing/routing is still required
Yes, VLAN membership overrides every mask
questions.explanation: Layer 2 connectivity and IP subnet membership are different. The scenario needs a suitable routing design for different subnets.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host has address 10.1.1.20/24 and gateway 10.1.1.1. Does that prove a router actually owns .1?
answers: No, the setting must be validated against the live network
Only if the DNS server is also .1
questions.explanation: A syntactically plausible gateway is not proof of ownership or reachability. Test ARP and the intended device configuration.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client can reach its gateway but not a remote server. What remains to be verified?
answers: Whether the client has any physical connection
Whether IPv4 exists on the client
Forward/return routing, policy and destination service
Whether the local gateway can ever reply
questions.explanation: Gateway success validates a limited local path. It does not establish the rest of the service path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A server has a valid static address but the DHCP pool can also lease that address. What is the risk?
answers: A lease may create a duplicate address unless allocation is coordinated
The server must become a DHCP relay
questions.explanation: Static addresses must be excluded or otherwise coordinated with dynamic allocation. Valid individual settings can still conflict.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client displays 0.0.0.0 while attempting DHCP. What should not be assumed?
answers: That it has a usable normal unicast host address
questions.explanation: 0.0.0.0 can represent an unspecified source during initial configuration. It is not an ordinary configured host address for normal service.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client's route table has a connected /24 and a default route. Which normally handles a destination inside that /24?
answers: The default route because it matches everything
questions.explanation: The connected prefix is more specific. The default is used when no more specific applicable route is selected.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A is 192.168.1.10/24; B is 192.168.1.130/25 on the same VLAN, without proxy ARP. How do they classify each other?
answers: A sees B as remote; B sees A as local
Both see each other as remote
Both see each other as local
A sees B as local; B sees A as remote
questions.explanation: A's /24 covers both. B's /25 covers .128-.255, so .10 is remote from B's perspective.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client uses /16 but the intended network is /24. It ARPs for a remote 10.1.2.50 rather than its gateway from 10.1.1.20. What explains this?
answers: The remote server must be on the same cable
The DNS server changed Ethernet addressing
The default gateway is always ignored for TCP
Its overly broad mask classifies the destination as on-link
questions.explanation: The incorrect connected prefix includes both third octets. With no proxy ARP or more specific route, the client seeks the destination locally.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host has connected 10.1.1.0/24 and a host route for 10.1.1.50/32 via a gateway. Which route normally wins for .50?
questions.explanation: Longest-prefix match selects the more specific host route. Do not assume connected routes always override every more specific prefix.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host has two default routes with equal prefix length and metrics 10 and 50. With no other policy, which is preferred?
answers: The route with the longer hostname
questions.explanation: For otherwise comparable host routes, lower effective metric is preferred. Real systems may combine interface and route metrics, so the scenario supplies effective values.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A VPN installs 10.0.0.0/8 while the local LAN has connected 10.1.1.0/24. Which route handles 10.1.1.50 by longest prefix?
questions.explanation: The /24 is more specific than /8. Overlapping private addressing can therefore divert traffic from the intended VPN destination.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Two organisations both use 192.168.1.0/24 and connect a VPN. What architectural issue arises?
answers: Private addresses become globally unique automatically
Overlapping address space can make destination identity/routing ambiguous
questions.explanation: Private space can be reused independently. Connecting those networks requires an explicit overlap solution, not just encryption.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A server receives remote requests but sends replies to an incorrect gateway. Which capture evidence supports this?
answers: Replies leave towards the wrong next-hop MAC
questions.explanation: The outgoing frame and route decision expose the wrong return next hop. Request arrival alone does not validate replies.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client has a valid lease but gateway ARP receives no reply. Which scope is strongest next?
answers: Only the public internet DNS root
Local VLAN/gateway presence and Layer 2 reachability
questions.explanation: ARP is a local-link dependency. Verify the intended VLAN, gateway interface and path before investigating remote application layers.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client ARPs successfully for its gateway but TCP to a remote server fails. What does ARP prove?
answers: The remote route is installed everywhere
Local address resolution to a MAC, not end-to-end service access
questions.explanation: ARP validates a limited local fact. It does not test the entire routed and filtered path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: Two MACs answer ARP for one server IP; captures show traffic alternating. What is the strongest supported hypothesis?
answers: A TCP checksum offload issue only
Duplicate address ownership or an explicitly designed redundancy mechanism needing verification
questions.explanation: Multiple ownership needs context: it may be a conflict or a deliberate mechanism. Verify the intended design before declaring either.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A DHCP client moves VLANs but retains an address from its old subnet. Physical link and new VLAN are correct. What correction should be investigated?
answers: Adding the old subnet to every switch blindly
Obtaining appropriate addressing for the new subnet
questions.explanation: Addressing must match the new Layer 3 network. Use approved renewal/configuration steps and verify the resulting options.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 10.1.1.20/24, gateway 10.1.1.1; the router's client interface is 10.1.2.1/24. What is wrong?
answers: The configured gateway does not match the router's local interface subnet
The host must use public DNS
questions.explanation: The host expects .1 in 10.1.1/24, but the router is on 10.1.2/24. Correct the intended subnet/gateway design, not unrelated DNS.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client has two NICs on different networks, and traffic exits the unintended NIC. What evidence is most useful?
answers: Route selection, effective metrics and source-interface choice
questions.explanation: Multihomed hosts can choose an unintended route. Inspect actual forwarding decisions instead of assuming the primary-looking adapter is used.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A traceroute hop times out but later hops and the destination respond. What is justified?
answers: The path necessarily stops at that hop
The client's subnet mask is certainly wrong
The non-responding hop did not provide the expected probe reply; transit still occurred
questions.explanation: Routers may filter or rate-limit diagnostic replies while forwarding traffic. Asterisks alone do not prove transit failure.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host pings a remote IP but names fail. Changing to public DNS restores public names but breaks internal names. Why?
answers: Public DNS always supplies private gateways
The public resolver may not know private internal DNS records
questions.explanation: Resolver choice affects available namespaces. Use the organisation's approved DNS design rather than treating public DNS as a universal fix.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: An address 169.254.20.30 appears on an adapter. Does that prove the central DHCP server is down?
answers: Yes, the VLAN must be correct
No, the client path, relay, scope or server may prevent obtaining a lease
Yes, APIPA uniquely diagnoses server power failure
questions.explanation: APIPA is a client symptom. Several dependencies can cause lease failure; isolate them with evidence.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client is 192.168.10.20/24 and its DNS server is 192.168.20.53. Is that DNS setting inherently invalid?
answers: No, a remote DNS server is usable if routing and policy permit it
Only if the DNS address ends in .1
Yes, DNS must always share the client subnet
Yes, DNS must equal the gateway
questions.explanation: Service servers can be remote. A gateway ordinarily needs local reachability, but DNS can be reached through routing.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host has a /32 interface address plus explicit on-link/next-hop routes. Must it behave like an ordinary /24 LAN host?
answers: Yes, every .1 address is automatically local
No, the supplied routes and interface model determine reachability
No, /32 cannot exist on any host
questions.explanation: Special interface models can use explicit routes with /32 addresses. Avoid applying conventional LAN assumptions without checking the route table.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client has 192.168.1.126/25. Which proposed ordinary host address shares its subnet?
questions.explanation: The subnet is .0-.127, with .1-.126 usable conventionally. The other addresses belong to the next subnet or are special there.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 10.2.7.200/22. What is its connected network?
questions.explanation: A /22 spans four third-octet values. Seven falls in the 4-7 block, so the network starts at 10.2.4.0.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host is 10.2.7.200/22. Which address is the directed broadcast for that subnet?
questions.explanation: The 10.2.4.0/22 range ends at 10.2.7.255. The mask determines the boundary, not the host's apparent /24.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A /24 network uses .254 as gateway and .1 as a server. Which claim is false?
answers: Both can be valid host addresses
IPv4 requires .1 to be the gateway
questions.explanation: There is no universal .1 gateway rule. Conventions must not be mistaken for protocol requirements.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client has valid IP settings, reaches its gateway, and DNS resolves correctly. An application still fails. What remains necessary?
answers: Assuming all network and application dependencies work
Testing the actual service path, port and application
Replacing the subnet mask without evidence
questions.explanation: Several successful preliminary tests do not validate the complete service. Follow the actual application's protocol and dependencies.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A host's route table has 192.168.0.0/16 via VPN and 192.168.10.0/24 locally. A desired remote host is 192.168.10.50. What is the overlap risk?
answers: The local /24 wins and may prevent reaching the intended remote address
The VPN /16 always overrides the local /24
questions.explanation: Longest-prefix match selects local /24. The same address space on both sides requires deliberate design to avoid ambiguity.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 addressing, private addresses and client configuration
questions.question: A client's static address matches a DHCP reservation for a different MAC. What should be investigated?
answers: Conflicting allocation intent and potential duplicate assignment
questions.explanation: A reservation associates an address with a client identity. A separate static owner can conflict with that allocation; coordinate the addressing plan.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: How many usable hosts are normally available in 10.30.4.0/24?
questions.explanation: /24 leaves 8 host bits. 2^8 gives 256 total addresses; subtract network and broadcast to get 254. This conventional rule excludes /31 and /32 special cases.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /24?
questions.explanation: /24 means 24 leading one-bits. Their dotted-decimal representation is 255.255.255.0; the prefix is not a host count.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the network address of 10.30.4.19/24?
questions.explanation: The address belongs to 10.30.4.0/24. Set the 8 host bits to zero to obtain 10.30.4.0; the host itself and broadcast are not the network address.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 10.30.4.0/24?
questions.explanation: The subnet has 256 addresses. Its final address, 10.30.4.255, has all host bits one; 10.30.4.254 is the last conventional usable host.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which ordinary host address belongs to 10.30.4.0/24?
questions.explanation: 10.30.4.1 lies inside the usable range. The network and broadcast are reserved in this conventional subnet; the remaining alternative lies outside it.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: How many usable hosts are normally available in 10.31.4.0/25?
questions.explanation: /25 leaves 7 host bits. 2^7 gives 128 total addresses; subtract network and broadcast to get 126. This conventional rule excludes /31 and /32 special cases.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /25?
questions.explanation: /25 means 25 leading one-bits. Their dotted-decimal representation is 255.255.255.128; the prefix is not a host count.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the network address of 10.31.4.19/25?
questions.explanation: The address belongs to 10.31.4.0/25. Set the 7 host bits to zero to obtain 10.31.4.0; the host itself and broadcast are not the network address.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 10.31.4.0/25?
questions.explanation: The subnet has 128 addresses. Its final address, 10.31.4.127, has all host bits one; 10.31.4.126 is the last conventional usable host.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which ordinary host address belongs to 10.31.4.0/25?
questions.explanation: 10.31.4.1 lies inside the usable range. The network and broadcast are reserved in this conventional subnet; the remaining alternative lies outside it.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: How many usable hosts are normally available in 10.32.4.0/26?
questions.explanation: /26 leaves 6 host bits. 2^6 gives 64 total addresses; subtract network and broadcast to get 62. This conventional rule excludes /31 and /32 special cases.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /26?
questions.explanation: /26 means 26 leading one-bits. Their dotted-decimal representation is 255.255.255.192; the prefix is not a host count.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the network address of 10.32.4.19/26?
questions.explanation: The address belongs to 10.32.4.0/26. Set the 6 host bits to zero to obtain 10.32.4.0; the host itself and broadcast are not the network address.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 10.32.4.0/26?
questions.explanation: The subnet has 64 addresses. Its final address, 10.32.4.63, has all host bits one; 10.32.4.62 is the last conventional usable host.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which ordinary host address belongs to 10.32.4.0/26?
questions.explanation: 10.32.4.1 lies inside the usable range. The network and broadcast are reserved in this conventional subnet; the remaining alternative lies outside it.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: How many usable hosts are normally available in 10.33.4.0/27?
questions.explanation: /27 leaves 5 host bits. 2^5 gives 32 total addresses; subtract network and broadcast to get 30. This conventional rule excludes /31 and /32 special cases.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /27?
questions.explanation: /27 means 27 leading one-bits. Their dotted-decimal representation is 255.255.255.224; the prefix is not a host count.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the network address of 10.33.4.19/27?
questions.explanation: The address belongs to 10.33.4.0/27. Set the 5 host bits to zero to obtain 10.33.4.0; the host itself and broadcast are not the network address.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 10.33.4.0/27?
questions.explanation: The subnet has 32 addresses. Its final address, 10.33.4.31, has all host bits one; 10.33.4.30 is the last conventional usable host.
questions.scope: CCNA calculated revision drill

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which ordinary host address belongs to 10.33.4.0/27?
questions.explanation: 10.33.4.1 lies inside the usable range. The network and broadcast are reserved in this conventional subnet; the remaining alternative lies outside it.

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: How many usable hosts are normally available in 10.34.4.0/28?
questions.explanation: /28 leaves 4 host bits. 2^4 gives 16 total addresses; subtract network and broadcast to get 14. This conventional rule excludes /31 and /32 special cases.

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /28?

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 10.34.4.0/28?

questions.topic: IPv4 subnetting, VLSM and summarisation
questions.question: Which ordinary host address belongs to 10.34.4.0/28?

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits. A typical /64 LAN prefix uses half for the prefix, but the complete address is still 128 bits.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which notation is normally used for IPv6 address groups?
questions.explanation: IPv6 text uses hexadecimal groups separated by colons. Dotted decimal is the familiar IPv4 format.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: How many 16-bit groups are in a fully expanded IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: Eight groups of 16 bits total 128 bits. Compression can hide zero groups without changing address length.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What can :: represent in an IPv6 address?
answers: One contiguous sequence of zero groups
questions.explanation: Double colon compresses consecutive zero groups. It cannot arbitrarily remove nonzero values.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: How many times can :: appear in one ordinary IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: Multiple occurrences would make expansion ambiguous. Leading zeroes in individual groups can be omitted separately.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which prefix identifies IPv6 link-local address space?
questions.explanation: FE80::/10 is link-local. Multicast and unique-local use different prefixes.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which prefix identifies IPv6 multicast?
questions.explanation: Multicast begins with FF. Link-local and unique-local are unicast categories, while ::1 is loopback.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What is IPv6 loopback?
questions.explanation: ::1 refers to the local host. :: is unspecified; FF02::1 is link-local all-nodes multicast.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What is the unspecified IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: All zero bits form the unspecified address. It is not a normal assigned destination address for a remote host.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Does IPv6 use an IP broadcast address?
answers: No, multicast provides relevant group-delivery functions
questions.explanation: IPv6 has no broadcast address. Do not apply IPv4 network/broadcast host subtraction mechanically to IPv6.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What does a unicast destination identify?
questions.explanation: Unicast addresses identify an interface. A device can have several addresses and interfaces.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What does anycast provide?
answers: Guaranteed delivery to the physically nearest server
Delivery to one of several interfaces sharing an address, selected by routing
questions.explanation: Anycast selects one reachable instance according to routing. It is not multicast or a geographic-distance guarantee.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What does multicast provide?
answers: Delivery to exactly one route-selected instance
Delivery to members of a specified group
A guarantee that every internet host receives traffic
A replacement for every unicast address
questions.explanation: Multicast addresses identify groups. Anycast instead selects one instance sharing an address.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which is an example of a unique-local IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: FD-prefixed addresses lie within unique-local space. Multicast, link-local and loopback have different purposes.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Can routers normally forward link-local traffic onto another link?
answers: Only if the host also has IPv4
Only if the address ends in ::1
questions.explanation: Link-local scope is restricted to the link. A link-local address can still identify a local router next hop.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What does /64 describe?
questions.explanation: The prefix length counts network bits. IPv6 remains 128 bits long.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What protocol family carries IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages?
questions.explanation: Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6. IPv6 does not use IPv4 ARP for neighbour resolution.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What does Neighbor Discovery help resolve on Ethernet?
questions.explanation: Neighbor Discovery performs local neighbour resolution and other functions. DNS name resolution is separate.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What is a Router Advertisement used for?
answers: Advertising router and link configuration information to hosts
questions.explanation: Router Advertisements can inform default-router and prefix configuration. They are not physical-link negotiation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What is SLAAC?
answers: Static Link Aggregation and Access Control
questions.explanation: SLAAC allows a host to form addresses using advertised prefix information and an interface identifier. It is not a DHCPv4 lease.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What is Duplicate Address Detection intended to check?
answers: Whether the default route has lowest cost
Whether the DNS server is public
Whether a tentative address is already in use on the link
questions.explanation: DAD checks local address uniqueness before ordinary use. It does not prove internet reachability.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: What does modified EUI-64 derive from a 48-bit MAC in the classic method?
questions.explanation: The method expands the MAC-derived identifier and flips the U/L bit. A network prefix is still needed to form the full address.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which value is inserted into a 48-bit MAC for classic modified EUI-64?
questions.explanation: FFFE is inserted between the original MAC halves. FE80 is associated with link-local prefixing, not the inserted identifier value.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which command gives a concise Cisco IOS IPv6 interface address/status view?
questions.explanation: The IPv6 interface brief command displays relevant IPv6 addressing and state. IPv4 ARP is not the IPv6 neighbour table.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Can one interface have both a link-local and a global IPv6 address?
answers: Only if it has two cables
questions.explanation: Multiple IPv6 addresses can coexist on an interface. Their scopes and roles differ.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which is equivalent to 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
questions.explanation: Zero compression and removal of leading zeroes preserve the value. Moving or changing nonzero groups does not.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which address text is invalid because of ambiguous compression?
questions.explanation: Two double-colon sequences cannot be expanded unambiguously. One is allowed.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Expand 2001:DB8:1:2::5. Which ending is correct?
questions.explanation: Four groups are written before :: and one after it, so three zero groups are inserted. The final value remains 5.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Are 2001:DB8:1:2::10 and 2001:DB8:1:2::20 in the same /64?
answers: No, different final values imply different prefixes
questions.explanation: The first four 16-bit groups match. Host identifiers can differ within the same /64.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Are 2001:DB8:1:2::10 and 2001:DB8:1:3::10 in the same /64?
answers: Yes, all 2001 addresses share a subnet
questions.explanation: The fourth group is part of the /64 prefix and differs. The shared host suffix does not establish subnet membership.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A host learns a default router from an RA. Which address commonly identifies that local router?
questions.explanation: Default-router discovery uses the advertising router's link-local address. It remains a local next hop for remote traffic.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A DHCPv6 server supplies an address but no RA or static default route exists. What can remain missing?
questions.explanation: DHCPv6 address assignment does not itself provide the normal RA-based default router. Addressing and routing must both be checked.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A host sends Router Solicitation. What response is it seeking?
answers: Neighbor Advertisement for a DNS name
questions.explanation: Router Solicitation requests router information. Neighbor Solicitation serves a different local discovery function.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A host needs the MAC for a local IPv6 neighbour. Which exchange is relevant?
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery rather than IPv4 ARP. The messages resolve local link-layer reachability.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An RA prefix has A=1 on a conventional Ethernet /64. What does A indicate?
answers: The router must be the only DNS server
The prefix may be used for autonomous address configuration
questions.explanation: The autonomous flag relates to SLAAC. Other RA fields independently describe on-link status and router lifetime.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An RA prefix has L=1. What does L indicate?
answers: The prefix is advertised as on-link
The client must use only DHCPv6
questions.explanation: The on-link flag concerns destination reachability on the link. It is distinct from the autonomous-address flag.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An RA has router lifetime zero but advertises a usable SLAAC prefix. What does zero lifetime mean?
answers: Do not use that advertiser as a default router based on this RA
questions.explanation: Router lifetime and prefix information are separate. A router can advertise prefix information without being a default router.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A tentative address fails DAD. What should be investigated?
answers: Another claimant or evidence causing duplicate detection
questions.explanation: DAD concerns local uniqueness. Do not force use of the address without understanding the conflict.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A host has only FE80::1234 and no other usable address or remote route. What scope is available?
questions.explanation: Link-local scope does not provide a globally routed source address. Local neighbour communication may still work.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A link-local ping on a multihomed host needs an interface identifier. Why?
answers: The interface name encrypts the packet
The same scoped address value can exist on different links
The address is a DNS alias
questions.explanation: The zone/interface identifies which link the scoped destination belongs to. The address alone may be ambiguous.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which IPv6 destination is link-local all-nodes multicast?
questions.explanation: FF02::1 identifies all nodes on the link. FF02::2 is all routers; ::1 is loopback.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which IPv6 destination is link-local all-routers multicast?
questions.explanation: The group identifies routers on the link. It is not a unicast gateway address.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A route uses FE80::1 as next hop. Which extra information is normally required?
questions.explanation: The next hop is link-scoped. The interface disambiguates which local link contains it.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which command configures a static IPv6 interface address in Cisco IOS interface mode?
questions.explanation: IPv6 interface syntax includes the prefix length. IPv4 dotted masks are not used for this command.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which global command enables IPv6 unicast forwarding on supported Cisco IOS devices?
questions.explanation: Address configuration and forwarding enablement are separate. Verify platform support and approved configuration before changes.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A router has IPv6 addresses but unicast forwarding is disabled. What may fail?
answers: Every local interface address must disappear
Transit routing between its IPv6 networks
DNS AAAA records must be deleted
questions.explanation: A device can have addresses without acting as an IPv6 transit router. Check forwarding configuration as well as addresses.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Classic modified EUI-64 starts from MAC 00:11:22:33:44:55. What identifier results?
questions.explanation: Insert FFFE between MAC halves and XOR the first octet with 0x02. The first octet changes from 00 to 02.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Classic modified EUI-64 starts from MAC 02:11:22:33:44:55. What is the first octet after U/L inversion?
questions.explanation: Flip the bit using XOR 0x02: 02 becomes 00. Do not always add two; inversion can clear an already-set bit.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Does a global-looking IPv6 address prove internet connectivity?
answers: No, routing and policy remain necessary
Yes, address type guarantees a working route
questions.explanation: Address type and connectivity are separate. The example documentation prefix also must not be treated as a real public allocation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A server has an AAAA record but its IPv6 service path fails while IPv4 works. What should be tested?
answers: Assume DNS is correct so all networking is healthy
IPv6 addressing, routes, policy and service separately
questions.explanation: An AAAA response supplies an IPv6 destination. It does not prove that path or listener is operational.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An RA has A=1, L=0 and a suitable /64 prefix. Which interpretation is correct?
answers: Autonomous address formation is permitted, but this option does not mark the prefix on-link
The prefix must be ignored because L is zero
Every destination in the prefix must be directly resolved
The flags are identical and both mean default router
questions.explanation: A and L have separate meanings. Do not infer on-link reachability solely from address formation.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An RA has A=0, L=1. What is advertised?
answers: An on-link prefix not authorised by that option for SLAAC address formation
A default route with no on-link information
questions.explanation: On-link determination and autonomous address generation are separate. Another mechanism can supply addresses.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A conventional Ethernet host uses a 64-bit interface identifier. An RA offers a /80 prefix for SLAAC. What is the issue?
answers: All /80 static addresses are universally invalid
Prefix length plus identifier length does not equal 128 bits for that method
The host should automatically shorten the identifier without support
questions.explanation: For the stated SLAAC method, the lengths must fit the address. This does not mean /80 can never be used in any other addressing model.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A host gets a valid DHCPv6 address and DNS settings, but no default router. Which dependency should be checked?
answers: Router Advertisements or explicitly configured routing
questions.explanation: DHCPv6 configuration does not replace normal default-router discovery. Separate address assignment from next-hop information.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An RA's router lifetime expires while the address remains valid. What can happen?
answers: The host loses that default-router entry while retaining the address
All neighbour entries must disappear immediately
questions.explanation: Router and address lifetimes govern different state. Address presence does not guarantee a usable remote route.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A SLAAC address is deprecated but still valid. What does that generally mean?
answers: It should not be preferred for new communication, though existing use may continue
It is immediately identical to an invalid address
It must be changed to multicast
questions.explanation: Preferred and valid lifetimes differ. Deprecation discourages new use; invalidation removes ordinary use.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A global IPv6 address is present, but the default router's neighbour entry remains incomplete. What scope is most relevant?
answers: Only the server's public DNS zone
Local next-hop resolution and link/policy behaviour
questions.explanation: A global address does not bypass local next-hop resolution. Investigate NS/NA and the local gateway path.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: IPv6 neighbour solicitations leave the host but no advertisements return; IPv4 ARP works. What should be investigated?
answers: Assume every IP protocol is permitted
Assume the whole Ethernet cable is unplugged
IPv6-specific multicast/ICMPv6 handling and neighbour configuration
questions.explanation: Working IPv4 proves some link operation, not IPv6 control traffic. Check protocol-specific policy and addressing.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A policy blocks all ICMPv6 but allows TCP 443. Why can HTTPS still fail?
answers: Allowing TCP creates neighbour entries automatically
Essential neighbour discovery or path-MTU signalling may be blocked
questions.explanation: ICMPv6 supports more than ping. Blanket filtering can break dependencies required before or during TCP communication.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Small IPv6 packets work; larger ones exceed a downstream MTU and Packet Too Big messages are blocked. What is plausible?
answers: Automatic fragmentation by every IPv6 router
A required change to link-local scope
questions.explanation: IPv6 routers do not fragment transit packets. The source needs usable path-MTU feedback to adapt.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A router receives an oversized IPv6 transit packet for its outgoing link. What should it normally do?
answers: Drop it and send ICMPv6 Packet Too Big as applicable
Fragment it like an IPv4 router
questions.explanation: IPv6 fragmentation is performed by sources, not transit routers. Packet Too Big provides the necessary feedback.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A ping to FE80::1 succeeds on interface A but fails on B. What does this establish?
answers: The IPv6 address is invalid because it repeats
Both tests must use the same neighbour
The address is globally unique everywhere
Reachability differs by link scope; identical address text need not identify one global device
questions.explanation: Link-local values can repeat on separate links. The interface/zone is part of interpreting the destination.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Two router interfaces on different links both use FE80::1. Is this inherently a duplicate-address conflict?
answers: Yes, link-local must be globally unique
Yes, both interfaces must use public addresses
No, uniqueness is evaluated within each link scope
questions.explanation: Repeated link-local values on separate links are allowed. A conflict would matter if the same scoped address is claimed on one link.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Two hosts on the same link claim the same unicast address and DAD reports a duplicate. What is appropriate?
answers: Investigate and resolve the ownership conflict before ordinary use
Disable DAD everywhere as the default fix
questions.explanation: DAD provides evidence of a local uniqueness problem. Removing the check does not remove the conflict.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An anycast address is assigned to two service instances. Which instance normally receives a packet?
answers: One selected by the routing path
questions.explanation: Anycast uses ordinary routing to choose one instance. Lowest routing cost is not necessarily shortest geographic distance.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Does anycast have a distinct address-text prefix that always identifies it?
answers: No, it uses unicast address space and deployment context
questions.explanation: Anycast cannot generally be identified from a unique textual prefix. Multicast has its own recognisable prefix.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: MAC 00:25:96:12:34:56 is used for classic modified EUI-64. Which identifier is correct?
questions.explanation: Split 002596 and 123456, insert FFFE, then flip the first-octet U/L bit. The ordering of inserted bytes matters.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: MAC C6:01:42:0F:00:07 is used for classic modified EUI-64. Which identifier is correct?
questions.explanation: C6 XOR 02 equals C4, not C8. Insert FFFE between the original three-byte halves.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: An IPv6 address lacks FFFE in its identifier. Does that prove it is invalid?
answers: Yes, all valid IPv6 addresses require FFFE
No, identifiers need not use the classic MAC-derived method
Yes, SLAAC requires that literal value universally
Only if it is global unicast
questions.explanation: Static, stable and privacy-oriented identifiers can differ. Modified EUI-64 is a method, not the only valid IPv6 addressing format.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Two /64 prefixes share the same interface identifier on different links. Is the complete address necessarily duplicated?
answers: Yes, prefixes are ignored by IPv6
Yes, only the identifier matters globally
No, different prefixes produce different complete addresses
questions.explanation: The complete 128-bit address includes prefix and identifier. Matching suffixes alone do not establish duplicate full addresses.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Which canonical compression is preferred for 2001:DB8:0:0:1:0:0:1 when zero runs tie?
questions.explanation: Canonical formatting compresses the longest zero run and the first when lengths tie. Multiple double colons are invalid; an alternative valid representation is not necessarily canonical.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A /48 allocation is divided into /64 LAN prefixes. How many /64s fit?
questions.explanation: The division adds 16 prefix bits. 2^16 equals 65,536; this counts subnets, not hosts.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: A /56 allocation is divided into /64 LAN prefixes. How many /64s fit?
questions.explanation: Eight additional prefix bits give 2^8 = 256 subnets. Do not subtract IPv4 network/broadcast reservations from this subnet count.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: Routes are 2001:DB8::/32 via A, 2001:DB8:10::/48 via B and 2001:DB8:10:20::/64 via C. Which handles 2001:DB8:10:20::5?
questions.explanation: The /64 is the longest matching installed prefix. Route-source preference does not override this more specific match.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: IPv6 addressing, address types, prefixes and modified EUI-64
questions.question: IPv4 HTTPS works, IPv6 DNS resolution works, but the IPv6 TCP handshake fails. What is the next justified focus?
answers: IPv6 service path, listener and policy rather than assuming DNS failure
Declare all networking healthy because IPv4 works
Assume AAAA resolution guarantees TCP success
questions.explanation: Dual-stack paths and policies can differ. A successful AAAA lookup supplies an address, not proof of IPv6 transport connectivity.
questions.scope: CCNA foundations and practical revision

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What does an SSID identify?
questions.explanation: An SSID names a WLAN. Association, authentication, VLAN mapping and IP configuration are separate requirements; a visible name is not proof of authorised service.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Which common 2.4 GHz channel plan uses non-overlapping 20 MHz channels?
questions.explanation: Channels 1, 6 and 11 are a common non-overlapping 20 MHz plan. Channel width and regulatory domain matter; neighbouring channel numbers are not independent spectrum.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What does RSSI describe?
questions.explanation: RSSI describes received RF signal strength. The scenario's threshold is supplied, not universal; noise, utilisation and client capability must also be considered.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What does SNR compare?
answers: TCP source port relative to destination
questions.explanation: SNR measures signal above noise. In the numerical example the difference is 30 dB; equal signal strength can yield different quality when noise differs.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What is co-channel contention?
questions.explanation: Devices sharing a channel contend for airtime. Strong signal alone does not guarantee capacity; distinguish this from overlapping adjacent-channel interference.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What is a trade-off of wider Wi-Fi channels?
answers: More spectrum per channel and fewer independent channel choices
questions.explanation: Wider channels can increase potential rate but consume more spectrum. They do not universally improve performance in a dense RF environment.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What does Wi-Fi encryption protect?
answers: Automatic safety of every internet application
Confidentiality of the protected wireless link
questions.explanation: Link encryption protects the wireless segment. It does not certify remote applications, remove endpoint risk or guarantee service performance.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What is the distinction between association and IP configuration?
answers: Wireless joining can succeed before usable IP configuration
APIPA proves all wireless authentication failed
questions.explanation: Joining the WLAN and obtaining usable IP settings are different stages. Check VLAN, relay and server paths when wireless joining succeeds but DHCP fails.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What does client roaming involve?
questions.explanation: Roaming concerns AP transitions. Authentication and handoff timing can affect service; strong RSSI alone does not prove seamless transition.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Does a high advertised Wi-Fi rate guarantee application throughput?
answers: PHY rate is not guaranteed application throughput
PHY rate equals usable throughput exactly
High PHY rate proves zero contention
High PHY rate validates all WAN links
questions.explanation: Protocol overhead, contention, retries and the rest of the path affect throughput. A displayed link rate is not an end-to-end performance measurement.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What does dBm express for RF power?
answers: They are equal because both are negative
questions.explanation: dBm is a logarithmic power measure relative to 1 mW. A less negative value is stronger; signal improvement does not alone establish application throughput.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What is adjacent-channel interference?
questions.explanation: Adjacent-channel overlap differs from co-channel airtime sharing. Channel width and regulatory planning affect the available choices.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: What is a BSSID in an ordinary infrastructure WLAN?
answers: The basic service set's identifier, commonly a MAC-format value
questions.explanation: BSSID distinguishes a basic service set; SSID is the WLAN name. Multiple APs can advertise the same SSID with different BSSIDs.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Does hidden SSID provide strong authentication?
answers: Hidden SSID eliminates all RF interception
The hidden name guarantees authorised access only
Hiding the name is not an authentication or encryption substitute
questions.explanation: SSID visibility is not a security credential. Use supported authentication and encryption rather than relying on name suppression.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Can more AP transmit power always improve a WLAN?
answers: A strong downlink proves a strong uplink
Both AP-to-client and client-to-AP RF paths matter
questions.explanation: Wireless communication is bidirectional. Excessive AP power can create an asymmetric usable range; assess client capabilities and the RF design.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Two WLANs share an AP but have different SSIDs. What distinguishes their advertised names?
questions.explanation: An SSID names a WLAN. Association, authentication, VLAN mapping and IP configuration are separate requirements; a visible name is not proof of authorised service.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Three nearby 2.4 GHz APs need a conventional 20 MHz plan. Which set is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Channels 1, 6 and 11 are a common non-overlapping 20 MHz plan. Channel width and regulatory domain matter; neighbouring channel numbers are not independent spectrum.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: A client reports weak received signal. Which measurement describes that signal strength?
questions.explanation: RSSI describes received RF signal strength. The scenario's threshold is supplied, not universal; noise, utilisation and client capability must also be considered.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Signal is -60 dBm and noise is -90 dBm. Which concept compares them?
answers: TCP source port relative to destination
questions.explanation: SNR measures signal above noise. In the numerical example the difference is 30 dB; equal signal strength can yield different quality when noise differs.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Two nearby APs use the same channel and defer transmission to each other. What is occurring?
questions.explanation: Devices sharing a channel contend for airtime. Strong signal alone does not guarantee capacity; distinguish this from overlapping adjacent-channel interference.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: An AP changes from 20 MHz to a wider channel. What spectrum trade-off should be considered?
answers: More spectrum per channel and fewer independent channel choices
questions.explanation: Wider channels can increase potential rate but consume more spectrum. They do not universally improve performance in a dense RF environment.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: A WLAN requires protected over-the-air payloads. Which function is relevant?
answers: Automatic safety of every internet application
Confidentiality of the protected wireless link
questions.explanation: Link encryption protects the wireless segment. It does not certify remote applications, remove endpoint risk or guarantee service performance.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: A laptop joins an SSID but receives APIPA. Which stage succeeded?
answers: APIPA proves all wireless authentication failed
Wireless joining can succeed before usable IP configuration
questions.explanation: Joining the WLAN and obtaining usable IP settings are different stages. Check VLAN, relay and server paths when wireless joining succeeds but DHCP fails.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: A client moves between AP coverage areas while using one WLAN. Which process is relevant?
questions.explanation: Roaming concerns AP transitions. Authentication and handoff timing can affect service; strong RSSI alone does not prove seamless transition.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: A client displays a high PHY rate but transfers slowly. What should be remembered?
answers: PHY rate is not guaranteed application throughput
High PHY rate proves zero contention
High PHY rate validates all WAN links
PHY rate equals usable throughput exactly
questions.explanation: Protocol overhead, contention, retries and the rest of the path affect throughput. A displayed link rate is not an end-to-end performance measurement.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: Which is stronger, -50 dBm or -75 dBm?
answers: They are equal because both are negative
questions.explanation: dBm is a logarithmic power measure relative to 1 mW. A less negative value is stronger; signal improvement does not alone establish application throughput.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: APs use overlapping 20 MHz channels 2 and 3. Which RF problem is plausible?
questions.explanation: Adjacent-channel overlap differs from co-channel airtime sharing. Channel width and regulatory planning affect the available choices.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: One SSID is advertised by several AP radios. Which identifier distinguishes a particular basic service set?
answers: The basic service set's identifier, commonly a MAC-format value
questions.explanation: BSSID distinguishes a basic service set; SSID is the WLAN name. Multiple APs can advertise the same SSID with different BSSIDs.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: A WLAN suppresses ordinary SSID advertisement. Does that replace encryption/authentication?
answers: The hidden name guarantees authorised access only
Hidden SSID eliminates all RF interception
Hiding the name is not an authentication or encryption substitute

questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: An AP is powerful but a low-power client cannot reliably send back. What must be considered?
answers: Both AP-to-client and client-to-AP RF paths matter
A strong downlink proves a strong uplink
questions.explanation: Wireless communication is bidirectional. Excessive AP power can create an asymmetric usable range; assess client capabilities and the RF design.
questions.scope: Original CCNA revision and practical scenarios

questions.topic: Wireless principles: RF, channels, SSIDs and encryption
questions.question: An SSID is visible but the client fails authentication. Which item identifies the WLAN without proving access permission?
questions.explanation: An SSID names a WLAN. Association, authentication, VLAN mapping and IP configuration are separate requirements; a visible name is not proof of authorised service.
